title: A survey on computer aided diagnosis for ocular diseases

subsections.section_title: Methodological Foundations and Data Resources
subsections.subsection_title: Population-Based Cohorts and Epidemiologic Study Design
subsections.content:
Population-based ophthalmic cohorts provide the sampling and inferential backbone for computer-aided diagnosis (CAD), because algorithmic validity depends on how disease prevalence, spectrum, and covariates are represented in the source population. Classic study designs span cross-sectional surveys for prevalence estimation and risk-factor discovery, exemplified by the Singapore Malay Eye Study (SiMES) and the Singapore Indian Eye Study (SINDI), as well as randomized prevention trials such as CAPT for age-related macular degeneration (AMD), which embed standardized longitudinal outcome ascertainment under controlled intervention conditions ref [1], ref [2], ref [3].

A recurring methodological strength of major eye cohorts is explicit sampling design. SiMES used age-stratified random sampling from a population registry of Malay adults aged 40–79 years, with centralized examinations, multimodal imaging, biospecimen collection, and prespecified handling of eligibility, noncontactability, and response enhancement strategies ref [1]. SINDI followed a closely related population-based framework in urban Indians, enabling cross-ethnic comparison of ocular traits under harmonized protocols ref [2]. Such registry-based, ethnicity-aware designs are especially valuable for CAD benchmarking because they reduce convenience-sampling bias and support subgroup analysis across refractive status, glaucoma risk, diabetic disease, and macular pathology.

Equally important is outcome definition and follow-up architecture. CAPT illustrates how rigorous epidemiologic design supports reliable labels through masked visual-function testing, centralized photograph reading, predefined adverse-event criteria, and long-term repeated assessments of acuity, lesion conversion, and vision-related quality of life ref [3]. Similar standardization principles were established in landmark epidemiologic programs such as the Beaver Dam Eye Study, the Blue Mountains Eye Study, and the Tanjong Pagar Survey, which helped define grading systems, prevalence estimates, and risk models for AMD, diabetic retinopathy, cataract, glaucoma, and refractive error ref [4], ref [5], ref [6], ref [7], ref [8]. For CAD surveys, these cohorts are foundational not only as data sources, but as exemplars of how sampling, masking, adjudication, and longitudinal design determine dataset reliability and downstream algorithm generalizability.

subsections.section_title: Methodological Foundations and Data Resources
subsections.subsection_title: Image Acquisition, Review Pipelines, and General Computational Foundations
subsections.content:
Image acquisition is the first methodological bottleneck in ocular CAD. Color fundus photography remains the workhorse for large-scale screening because of its relatively low cost and compatibility with telemedicine, while multimodal extensions such as fluorescein angiography, confocal scanning, and optical coherence tomography broaden structural and vascular assessment when available [1]. However, downstream performance is highly contingent on acquisition variability, including blur, nonuniform illumination, camera-dependent color shifts, field-of-view differences, and pigmentation-related contrast changes, making preprocessing and quality control integral rather than optional components of CAD pipelines [1].

Accordingly, review pipelines typically begin with image quality assessment and standardization before lesion-specific analysis. Illumination and contrast normalization are commonly used to suppress low-frequency shading and improve comparability across visits and devices, with classical retinal normalization models showing clear utility for subsequent segmentation and registration [1]. Image quality screening is equally important in teleophthalmology settings, where no-reference sharpness metrics and anisotropy-based measures can flag ungradable images before referral or algorithmic triage [1]. For wider retinal coverage, multi-view registration and mosaicking have also been explored; SIFT-based pipelines combined with robust outlier rejection can align overlapping fundus views and construct enlarged mosaics, although geometric distortion and sparse texture remain practical challenges [2].

At the computational level, many ophthalmic CAD systems still follow a common backbone: oversegmentation or candidate generation, feature extraction, supervised classification, and post hoc structural reasoning. More general vision work on learning-based segmentation is relevant here because it formalized segmentation as classification over contour, texture, brightness, and continuity cues, providing a conceptual basis for later retinal region partitioning and object delineation [3]. In practice, this foundation supports classical machine-learning schemes for vessel, disc, and lesion analysis, and also interfaces naturally with contemporary end-to-end deep learning by framing acquisition artifacts, annotation noise, and review-stage uncertainty as part of the same statistical decision pipeline [1], [3].

subsections.section_title: Methodological Foundations and Data Resources
subsections.subsection_title: Retinal Lesion Detection for Diabetic Retinopathy and Macular Disease
subsections.content:
Retinal lesion detection for diabetic retinopathy (DR) has historically centered on identifying red lesions—especially microaneurysms and small hemorrhages—and bright lesions such as hard exudates. Classical pipelines typically combine green-channel enhancement, candidate extraction, vessel suppression, and candidate classification. Early morphology-driven systems demonstrated that carefully engineered features could support lesion-level screening before the widespread adoption of deep learning ref [8], while more specialized detectors exploited local contrast normalization to better separate true microaneurysms from background texture and vessel-associated dark spots ref [8]. Frequency-domain formulations were also explored; for example, curvelet-based enhancement was used to suppress background structure and isolate red lesions with explicit vessel subtraction ref [7].

A recurring methodological theme is the generation of high-sensitivity candidate sets followed by false-positive reduction. Microaneurysm detectors based on local rotating cross-section profile analysis modeled lesion appearance through directional peak statistics and achieved competitive results in public challenges ref [13]. Ensemble formulations further improved robustness by combining preprocessing methods and candidate extractors rather than only classifier outputs, yielding strong microaneurysm detection and useful image-level DR grading performance ref [9]. For exudates, morphology-based candidate selection was refined by active contours and regionwise boosted classification to better recover irregular lesion boundaries while reducing confusion with the optic disc and reflective background structures ref [10].

Macular disease has also been addressed through lesion-oriented fundus analysis, particularly for age-related macular degeneration (AMD). In this setting, drusen detection methods used macula localization, grading overlays, vessel suppression, and regional intensity analysis in RGB/HSV spaces to identify deposits associated with AMD risk ref [9]. Collectively, these studies established core CAD principles still visible in later systems: lesion-specific preprocessing, anatomy-aware masking, multistage candidate pruning, and evaluation at both lesion and image levels across public datasets such as DIARETDB1, ROC, and Messidor ref [7], ref [9], ref [10], ref [13], ref [8].

subsections.section_title: Methodological Foundations and Data Resources
subsections.subsection_title: Optic Disc, Cup, and Peripapillary Structure Analysis
subsections.content:
Analysis of the optic disc, cup, and adjacent peripapillary tissue is central to computer-aided glaucoma assessment because structural cupping, rim loss, and parapapillary changes are among the earliest visible biomarkers. Early work on disc/cup delineation exploited stereo color photographs, where physiologically inspired pixel features and disparity cues enabled automated cup, rim, and background labeling with strong agreement to expert planimetry, highlighting the value of depth-sensitive representations for linear cup-to-disc ratio estimation ref [14]. In parallel, monocular fundus approaches sought to compensate for missing depth by combining region statistics, shape constraints, and vessel-based anatomical cues, culminating in integrated disc-and-cup pipelines tailored to glaucoma screening ref [19].

Cup segmentation from 2D fundus images proved particularly challenging because pallor is an imperfect surrogate of excavation. Accordingly, several methods turned to clinically motivated geometric evidence at the cup boundary. Vessel kinking was explicitly modeled as a sign of contour descent within the cup and combined with pallor information to improve horizontal cup-width estimation ref [17]. Level-set formulations were also adopted for automatic cup-to-disc ratio computation, typically followed by ellipse fitting to regularize boundaries distorted by vessel crossings and weak gradients ref [8]. Beyond monocular imagery, multiview and sequential fundus acquisitions enabled depth-discontinuity-based boundary inference, avoiding strict stereo calibration while still improving cup-to-disc ratio and cup area estimates over monocular baselines ref [18].

Peripapillary structures provide complementary context. Peripapillary atrophy has been modeled using sparse biologically inspired feature manifolds, demonstrating that tissue immediately surrounding the disc contains diagnostically useful cues for myopia- and glaucoma-related assessment ref [20]. Likewise, population-based OCT studies established normative distributions of peripapillary retinal nerve fibre layer thickness and confirmed systematic variation with age, refractive error, disc size, rim area, and parapapillary beta zone, thereby supplying critical reference ranges for structure-aware CAD systems ref [9]. Taken together, these studies show a methodological progression from boundary extraction and handcrafted appearance modeling toward anatomically grounded, multimodal quantification of the optic nerve head and its peripapillary environment ref [14], ref [17], ref [19].

subsections.section_title: Methodological Foundations and Data Resources
subsections.subsection_title: Retinal Vessel and Myopia-Oriented Structural Biomarkers
subsections.content:
Retinal vasculature provides a complementary biomarker family to lesion-centric analysis, capturing both systemic microvascular change and eye-specific structural remodeling. Early vessel extraction methods modeled vessels as elongated Gaussian-like ridges, using matched filtering with adaptive probing to improve continuity and suppress pathology-induced false positives, thereby establishing a practical basis for quantifying vessel caliber, branching, and tortuosity from fundus photographs ref [21]. Tracking-oriented formulations further exploited steerable filters to follow vessel centerlines, estimate local direction, and recover contours, linking segmentation directly to downstream morphometry such as diameter and branch analysis ref [24].

Beyond segmentation, several studies emphasized that diagnosis-relevant vascular phenotypes depend on precise geometric measurement rather than binary masks alone. In particular, subpixel vessel-width estimation using 2-D Gaussian or difference-of-Gaussian models improved robustness to central light reflexes and local background variation, outperforming earlier half-height and rectangular-profile schemes in precision ref [22]. Such measurement pipelines are clinically pertinent because caliber variation, venous beading, and related width irregularities are hallmarks in diabetic and hypertensive retinopathy, while vessel-course tracking enables contour-based assessment of tortuosity and branching abnormalities ref [22], ref [24].

For myopia-oriented CAD, structural biomarkers around the optic nerve head became especially important. PAMELA operationalized pathological myopia detection using optic-disc tilt, peripapillary atrophy (PPA), and regional texture asymmetry around the disc, combining these handcrafted indicators in an SVM classifier and demonstrating that disc-centered structural analysis can support screening from color fundus images ref [25]. A later bag-of-features and sparse-learning approach moved beyond explicit handcrafted lesion rules, learning discriminative local fundus patterns associated with pathological myopia at scale and achieving strong population-based recognition performance ref [6]. Together, these studies illustrate a progression from vessel and peripapillary morphology engineered from geometric models toward data-driven representations of myopia-related structural change ref [25], ref [6].

subsections.section_title: Computer-Aided Diagnosis Based on Clinical and Imaging Data
subsections.subsection_title: Knowledge-Based and Multimodal CAD Frameworks
subsections.content:
Knowledge-based CAD frameworks in ophthalmology predate contemporary machine learning and were motivated by the need to encode expert reasoning explicitly. Early consultation systems such as CASNET/EXPERT demonstrated how causal, hierarchical disease representations could support diagnostic inference and explanation, establishing an important conceptual foundation for ophthalmic decision support beyond pure pattern recognition ref [26]. Later work on computer-based classification of eye diseases extended this paradigm to image-derived feature spaces, comparing neural, fuzzy, and neuro-fuzzy classifiers for differentiating normal eyes from cataract, iridocyclitis, and corneal haze, and illustrating the appeal of interpretable hybrid reasoning in small clinical datasets ref [32].

A second line of development emphasized probabilistic and retrieval-based knowledge integration. Tobin et al. proposed a content-based diagnostic framework in which posterior disease probabilities were inferred from visually similar fundus images in an annotated archive, thereby combining image semantics with prior class distributions rather than relying on a single lesion detector ref [30]. For diabetic retinopathy, Niemeijer et al. explicitly studied information fusion across lesion detectors, image-quality assessment, and multiple views per examination, showing that supervised fusion at exam level substantially affected screening performance and was essential for prescreening deployment ref [31]. These studies highlighted a recurring survey theme: clinically useful CAD often depends as much on how heterogeneous evidence is fused as on the performance of individual component algorithms ref [30], ref [31].

Recent multimodal frameworks further broadened the evidence base to combine imaging with clinical, functional, and even genomic data. In glaucoma, fusion of standard automated perimetry and OCT using anatomically informed structure-function mappings improved automated diagnosis relative to SAP alone, showing the value of embedding prior physiological knowledge into classifier inputs ref [27]. Related medical imaging informatics approaches integrated retinal image features, personal variables, and SNPs through multiple kernel learning, outperforming single-source glaucoma screening strategies such as intraocular pressure alone ref [8]. A similar trend was reported for pathological myopia, where heterogeneous fusion of fundus images, demographic/clinical variables, and genotyping data improved AUC over individual sources, suggesting that multimodal CAD is particularly advantageous for ocular diseases with both phenotypic and systemic or genetic determinants ref [28].

subsections.section_title: Computer-Aided Diagnosis Based on Clinical and Imaging Data
subsections.subsection_title: Cataract and Other Ocular Disorder Classification
subsections.content:
Cataract CAD has developed largely along two imaging pathways: slit-lamp photography for nuclear cataract and retro-illumination imaging for cortical and posterior subcapsular cataracts (PSC). Early objective systems for nuclear opacification relied on handcrafted photometric descriptors extracted from the visual axis or a circular nuclear region, using regression or neural-network classifiers to emulate clinical grading systems such as Wilmer, Wisconsin, and LOCS-style protocols ref [38], ref [37]. These studies were important because they demonstrated that objective image-derived measures could improve reproducibility over manual assessment, while also revealing the limits of sparse axial features for representing the full nucleus opacity pattern ref [38], ref [37].

Subsequent slit-lamp CAD frameworks moved toward explicit anatomical modeling of the lens and nucleus. A computer-aided diagnosis system of nuclear cataract combined modified active shape models, clinically motivated intensity/color/texture features, and support vector regression, and was validated on more than 5000 images, indicating that large-scale automatic grading was feasible in population studies ref [37]. Huang et al. further reformulated nuclear cataract grading as a ranking problem rather than simple classification or regression, learning an image order consistent with clinical severity and then interpolating grades from neighboring cases; on 1000 slit-lamp images, this ranking-based strategy outperformed earlier grading-by-classification and grading-by-regression baselines ref [33].

For retro-illumination images, CAD has focused on opacity segmentation and screening. Li et al. proposed a rule-based PSC detector combining pupil localization, global and local thresholding, edge cues, size filtering, and spatial priors, achieving preliminary screening sensitivity/specificity of 82.6%/80.0% ref [36]. Texture-centered approaches then became prominent: enhanced local-entropy features on paired anterior/posterior images supported cataract-versus-noncataract discrimination for mass screening, with 84.8% accuracy on 4545 image pairs ref [7], while later texture-and-intensity analysis improved ROI detection, lens masking, and dense-opacity handling for cortical and PSC detection ref [8]. Taken together, these studies show a characteristic evolution in cataract CAD from handcrafted densitometric rules to structure-aware and texture-aware models, with increasing attention to robustness under uneven illumination, artifacts, and mixed cataract morphology ref [36], ref [7], ref [8].

subsections.section_title: Computer-Aided Diagnosis Based on Clinical and Imaging Data
subsections.subsection_title: Age-Related Macular Degeneration and Pathological Myopia
subsections.content:
Computer-aided diagnosis for age-related macular degeneration (AMD) has largely evolved along two complementary lines: lesion-centric drusen analysis and direct image-level grading. Early work emphasized explicit drusen segmentation, for example via geodesic reconstruction and mathematical morphology to delineate bright deposits under challenging background variation ref [41]. Subsequent systems refined drusen quantification for AMD classification from color fundus photographs, combining preprocessing, illumination normalization, and supervised learning to improve robustness across acquisition conditions ref [16].

A parallel trend moved from lesion extraction toward holistic AMD recognition. Image-mining and graph-based representations enabled highly accurate disease/no-disease grading without requiring fully interpretable lesion segmentation, highlighting the value of spatial context and data-driven feature discovery ref [40]. Other studies pursued direct grading of macular degeneration from color fundus images by integrating macular localization with lesion overlap analysis, while probabilistic classifiers were also explored to distinguish normal eyes from dry and wet AMD patterns ref [45], ref [10]. Collectively, these studies show the transition from handcrafted drusen measurements to broader classification pipelines that better tolerate heterogeneous image quality and phenotype variability ref [40], ref [16].

For pathological myopia, CAD methods initially focused on clinically meaningful surrogates such as peripapillary atrophy (PPA). The PAMELA framework demonstrated that texture descriptors extracted around the optic disc, combined with SVM classification, can detect pathological myopia with promising sensitivity and specificity ref [17]. A related variational level-set formulation modeled the difference between internal and external disc boundaries to localize PPA more explicitly ref [18]. More recent work broadened the representation beyond PPA alone, using bag-of-features and sparse learning on large population-based datasets to capture multiple retinal changes associated with pathological myopia and to achieve strong AUC and balanced accuracy ref [43]. These results suggest that, for both AMD and pathological myopia, robust CAD increasingly depends on combining clinically grounded priors with data-driven visual representations ref [43], ref [17], ref [18].

subsections.section_title: Computer-Aided Diagnosis Based on Clinical and Imaging Data
subsections.subsection_title: Diabetic Retinopathy CAD and Lesion Detection
subsections.content:
Diabetic retinopathy (DR) CAD has evolved along two tightly coupled directions: image-level screening for referable disease and lesion-level analysis targeting early vascular abnormalities, especially microaneurysms (MAs). Early systems emphasized automated red-lesion detection in screening populations and showed that adjustable operating points could trade sensitivity against specificity for practical referral workflows in both film-based and digital settings ref [16], ref [17]. Subsequent screening-oriented studies extended this paradigm from any-DR detection to referable DR and maculopathy, integrating lesion evidence with image quality assessment and clinically meaningful referral rules around the macula ref [12], ref [14].

At the lesion level, MA detection became a central benchmark because MAs are often the earliest visible sign of DR. Representative approaches include local contrast normalization with explicit vessel handling to reduce false positives on vascular structures ref [9], sparse-representation classification with learned MA/non-MA dictionaries ref [48], and ensemble strategies that combine multiple preprocessing and candidate-extraction modules for more robust MA detection and DR grading ref [18]. These works reflect a broader methodological shift from handcrafted morphology and filtering toward learned dictionaries, classifier fusion, and confidence-based candidate aggregation.

Beyond single-time-point analysis, longitudinal CAD has also been explored for monitoring progression or regression of DR lesions. Robust registration, illumination correction, and Bayesian change analysis enabled direct detection and classification of temporal retinal changes, showing the value of CAD not only for screening but also for follow-up assessment ref [46]. More recent large-scale validation studies further demonstrated that integrated systems can achieve high sensitivity for referable DR on externally collected cohorts, supporting the feasibility of automated triage in clinical screening pipelines ref [14]. Overall, DR CAD illustrates how lesion detection, image quality control, and referral-oriented decision logic must be jointly optimized for safe deployment ref [12], ref [16], ref [17].

subsections.section_title: Computer-Aided Diagnosis Based on Clinical and Imaging Data
subsections.subsection_title: Glaucoma Diagnosis from Structural Imaging and Clinical Measurements
subsections.content:
Glaucoma CAD has evolved from heuristic assessment of optic nerve appearance toward quantitative models that integrate structural imaging and clinical measurements. Early clinically interpretable rules remain important baselines: the ISNT configuration of neuroretinal rim thickness differentiates many normal from glaucomatous discs, but its violations are neither perfectly sensitive nor specific, motivating automated analysis beyond simple cup-to-disc inspection ref [54]. In parallel, learning-based analysis of standard automated perimetry showed that machine-learning classifiers such as SVMs and neural networks can outperform conventional summary indices, illustrating the value of multivariate modeling of glaucomatous structure-function change ref [52].

On fundus photography, a major line of work estimates optic disc, cup, and rim geometry for structural assessment. Automated optic nerve analysis has used abstract shape descriptors and feature selection on confocal scanning laser tomographic images to distinguish healthy from glaucomatous eyes ref [57]. For color fundus images, methods range from appearance-based glaucoma risk scoring without explicit segmentation ref [16] to dedicated disc/cup delineation. Notably, monocular image approaches have combined robust disc segmentation with vessel-bend cues for cup localization, enabling vertical and area cup-to-disc measurements for glaucoma assessment ref [56]. Stereo-photograph methods further exploit depth disparity to derive cup and disc boundaries, yielding clinically useful cup-to-disc ratios for discriminating glaucomatous from nonglaucomatous eyes ref [58].

OCT has further strengthened structural CAD by providing direct three-dimensional characterization of the optic nerve head. Graph-theoretic methods have been proposed to segment the optic disc margin from volumetric SD-OCT using Bruch’s membrane opening projections and vessel-aware cost modification ref [18]. Related voxel-column classification frameworks segment cup and rim directly from SD-OCT volumes, with cup-to-disc ratios correlating closely with expert stereo planimetry ref [20]. More broadly, automated glaucoma diagnosis benefits from combining such structural descriptors with complementary measurements, and multimodal fusion of OCT with perimetric data has been shown to improve diagnostic performance over single-source analysis ref [35].

subsections.section_title: Genetic Prediction and Genomic Knowledge Discovery for Ocular Diseases
subsections.subsection_title: Heritability and Twin Studies of Ocular Traits
subsections.content:
Twin and family designs provided the earliest quantitative evidence that many ocular phenotypes are substantially heritable, while also revealing trait-specific environmental contributions. In age-related macular degeneration (AMD), the large US veteran twin study showed significant additive genetic effects for overall severity and for intermediate and advanced disease, with heritability estimates rising from about 0.46 for ordinal grade to 0.67–0.71 for more severe phenotypes, while unique environment remained non-negligible and shared environment was limited ref [59]. Similar twin-based decomposition in age-related nuclear cataract found that additive genetics explained roughly 48% of variation, with age accounting for much of the remainder and common environment contributing little ref [9].

Highly heritable quantitative endophenotypes were also identified. Central corneal thickness, a clinically important parameter for glaucoma risk assessment and intraocular pressure interpretation, showed near-complete familial resemblance in monozygotic pairs and an estimated heritability of 0.95 in a multicenter twin study ref [61]. Refractive traits likewise displayed strong genetic determination. A population-based twin study in adults aged 20–45 years estimated heritability of about 0.89–0.94 for refraction, axial length, and corneal curvature, with evidence suggestive of gene–environment interaction despite weak effects of educational discordance within pairs ref [10]. Complementarily, the Finnish Twin Cohort study reported substantial heritability for hyperopia, around 0.75, especially for higher degrees of farsightedness ref [8].

Not all ocular diseases showed equally strong twin-based heritability. In a Finnish population-based linkage study of chronic open-angle glaucoma, concordance differences between monozygotic and dizygotic pairs suggested a genetic role, but the estimated heritability was modest at approximately 13%, underscoring phenotypic heterogeneity and the importance of age-dependent expression, diagnostic variability, and nonshared exposures ref [64]. Taken together, these studies established two enduring lessons for ocular genomics: first, endophenotypes such as corneal thickness and refractive components may be more genetically tractable than broad clinical syndromes; second, even for strongly heritable traits, unique environmental effects remain relevant, motivating later gene discovery and risk-prediction efforts.

subsections.section_title: Genetic Prediction and Genomic Knowledge Discovery for Ocular Diseases
subsections.subsection_title: Genetic Architecture of Major Ocular Diseases
subsections.content:
The genetic architecture of major ocular diseases is heterogeneous, spanning rare high-penetrance mutations, common polygenic susceptibility, and measurable intermediate traits. In age-related macular degeneration (AMD), this architecture is now understood as a prototypical example of a common complex disease in which complement regulation, lipid metabolism, extracellular matrix remodeling, and inflammatory pathways all contribute to risk; major loci such as CFH and the ARMS2/HTRA1 region account for substantial but incomplete heritability, implying extensive polygenicity and gene–environment interplay, particularly with aging and smoking exposures ref [65], ref [5], ref [6].

Primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) similarly combines rare Mendelian forms with broader complex inheritance. Early linkage studies identified genes such as MYOC and OPTN for uncommon familial cases, but population risk is better captured through endophenotypes including intraocular pressure (IOP) and vertical cup-to-disc ratio (VCDR). Extended pedigree analyses indicate that IOP and VCDR are not only heritable, but genetically correlated with POAG, supporting their role as biologically proximal traits for gene discovery; by contrast, central corneal thickness, although highly heritable, may be a weaker disease endophenotype than initially assumed ref [66], ref [7], ref [8], ref [9].

For refractive error and myopia, the prevailing architecture is strongly polygenic and developmentally contingent. Family history is among the most consistent predictors, twin-based modeling suggests high heritability, and both common susceptibility loci and rare variants contribute across the severity spectrum, with high/pathologic myopia showing greater enrichment of rare familial loci. At the same time, the phenotype is unusually sensitive to environmental modulation, especially educational intensity and near-work related exposures, making myopia a canonical example of gene–environment correlation and interaction in ocular disease ref [4], ref [10], ref [11], ref [12].

Across these diseases, a unifying theme is that dissecting quantitative ocular traits can simplify otherwise heterogeneous clinical endpoints. AMD benefits from pathway-based interpretation of large-effect common loci, glaucoma from genetically informative structural and pressure-related endophenotypes, and myopia from integrating developmental ocular biometry with genomic susceptibility. This layered view of architecture is especially relevant for computer-aided diagnosis, because imaging phenotypes may function not only as diagnostic markers but also as genetically anchored traits that bridge molecular discovery and clinically actionable disease subtyping ref [65], ref [66], ref [4], ref [13].

subsections.section_title: Genetic Prediction and Genomic Knowledge Discovery for Ocular Diseases
subsections.subsection_title: Genetic Prediction and Clinical Translation
subsections.content:
Genetic prediction aims to translate genomic discovery into individualized estimates of disease susceptibility, but clinical deployment requires more than statistical association. Early frameworks for predictive genetic testing emphasized that analytic validity, clinical validity, and clinical utility must all be established before routine use, with particular attention to representative populations, post-test interventions, counseling, and external review of test performance ref [68]. These translational requirements are especially relevant in ophthalmology, where many common disorders are genetically complex and where preventive or monitoring strategies differ across age-related macular degeneration, glaucoma, diabetic retinopathy, cataract, and refractive error.

From a modeling perspective, GWAS-derived prediction is constrained by the small effect sizes of most common variants, yet performance can improve when many loci are combined rather than restricting models to genome-wide significant hits alone ref [69]. Kooperberg et al. showed that sparse regression approaches such as the lasso can yield better-calibrated risk models than simple top-hit selection, provided that SNP preselection and model fitting are strictly separated between training and test data to avoid optimistic bias and the "winner's curse" ref [69]. More broadly, theoretical and empirical evaluations of polygenic profiling indicate that predictive discrimination depends on disease heritability, allele-frequency spectrum, training sample size, and the proportion of variance captured by known loci, so current scores are often more useful for risk stratification than stand-alone diagnosis ref [69].

For ocular diseases, the most immediate clinical translation of genetic prediction is likely in prognosis enrichment, screening personalization, and trial design rather than deterministic patient-level decision making. In practice, genomic risk scores will be most informative when integrated with age, family history, ancestry, lifestyle exposures, and image-derived phenotypes from fundus photography or OCT, rather than used in isolation. Thus, the translational path for ocular genomics is less about replacing clinical examination and more about building calibrated multimodal risk models whose benefit, fairness, and actionability are prospectively validated in diverse populations before adoption ref [68], ref [69].

subsections.section_title: Genetic Prediction and Genomic Knowledge Discovery for Ocular Diseases
subsections.subsection_title: Genome-wide Association and Statistical Methods for Genomic Discovery
subsections.content:
Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) established a scalable framework for genomic discovery by combining dense SNP arrays, stringent quality control, and explicit correction for population structure and multiplicity. Early scans also highlighted core design principles still relevant to ocular genetics, including replication across cohorts, genomic control, false-discovery-rate filtering, and the importance of linkage disequilibrium for signal interpretation and fine-mapping; these lessons generalize from landmark complex-trait studies to ophthalmic phenotypes and diseases ref [71].

Methodologically, a major shift has been from single-marker testing toward joint modeling of many variants. Lasso-based regularization provided the conceptual basis for sparse selection in high-dimensional settings ref [74], and was subsequently adapted to penalized logistic regression for GWAS-scale case-control analysis ref [75]. Related multivariate strategies, including simultaneous SNP modeling and Bayesian-inspired shrinkage, improve localization and can reduce redundant signals in regions of strong LD ref [77]. Power can also be increased by biologically informed filtering, as exemplified by prioritized subset analysis and pathway-guided interaction screening ref [10].

A second frontier is interaction discovery. Exhaustive two-locus testing remains computationally prohibitive at GWAS scale, motivating efficient algorithms such as TEAM for contingency-table-based epistasis scans ref [72]. Hybrid procedures such as screen-and-clean use staged lasso screening followed by confirmatory testing to control type I error while exploring interaction models ref [73], and LASSO-PCA combinations further target gene-gene interactions in ultra-high-dimensional data ref [9]. Together, these approaches define a practical statistical toolbox for ocular genomic discovery, where modest marginal effects, polygenicity, and potential interaction structure demand methods beyond conventional single-SNP association tests ref [3,4,6,8].

subsections.section_title: Genetic Prediction and Genomic Knowledge Discovery for Ocular Diseases
subsections.subsection_title: Broader Genetic Models and Comparative Perspectives
subsections.content:
Beyond conventional additive single-locus models, ocular genetics increasingly benefits from broader frameworks that accommodate cross-trait correlation, non-Mendelian architecture, and comparative evidence across species. Comparative ophthalmic genetics is particularly informative because many eye phenotypes are conserved, while breed structures in domestic animals can amplify inherited risk and clarify segregation patterns that are difficult to resolve in heterogeneous human cohorts. In this respect, analyses of presumed inherited eye diseases in Entlebucher Mountain Dogs showed measurable heritability for noncongenital cataract and progressive retinal atrophy, together with a moderate positive genetic correlation between the two traits, illustrating how liability models can reveal shared genetic influences across ocular phenotypes even outside human populations ref [2].

These comparative studies also highlight methodological lessons relevant to human ocular genomics. In the canine study, threshold animal models yielded larger heritability estimates than linear models, and estimates were sensitive to diagnostic expertise and ascertainment practices, underscoring that phenotype definition and observer reliability materially affect inferred genetic architecture ref [2]. Similar concerns apply in human studies of refraction, glaucoma endophenotypes, cataract, and age-related macular degeneration, where broad-sense genetic models may need to incorporate gene-gene interaction, pleiotropy, rare variation, and gene-environment interplay rather than relying only on common-variant additive effects.

From a survey perspective, comparative genetics therefore expands genomic knowledge discovery in ocular disease in two ways. First, animal populations provide quasi-experimental structures for dissecting inherited eye disorders and for testing multivariate and threshold-based models of disease liability ref [2]. Second, they offer a translational perspective: although species-specific effects limit direct extrapolation, convergent phenotypes such as retinal degeneration and cataract support the search for shared pathways, modifier mechanisms, and more robust phenotype models that can complement human GWAS and polygenic prediction.

subsections.section_title: Emerging Trends, Synthesis, and Conclusions
subsections.subsection_title: From Structural OCT Segmentation to Robust Ophthalmic Biomarkers
subsections.content:
A clear trend in ophthalmic CAD is the shift from structural OCT segmentation as an end in itself toward anatomically grounded biomarkers. Early work on optic nerve head OCT focused on delineating clinically familiar structures such as the disc margin, cup, and rim, often by converting volumetric data into constrained 2D or quasi-3D optimization problems. Graph-theoretic segmentation of the optic disc margin in 3D OCT demonstrated that Bruch’s membrane opening-related boundaries could be localized reproducibly, while suppressing vessel-induced artifacts through projection-based cost design ref [57]. Closely related methods for automated cup and rim segmentation from spectral-domain OCT further showed that OCT-derived cup-to-disc estimates correlate strongly with expert planimetry, helping bridge legacy clinical concepts and volumetric imaging ref [79].

The more important conceptual advance, however, was the move from photograph-like surrogates to stable anatomic reference structures. Automated segmentation of the neural canal opening (NCO) and optic cup at the RPE/Bruch’s membrane level explicitly reframed biomarker extraction around a potentially more reproducible landmark than the subjective clinical disc margin ref [4]. This direction is consistent with morphometric studies showing that the visible disc margin may correspond variably to Bruch’s membrane termination, border tissue, or scleral canal anatomy, limiting the biological specificity of conventional planimetry. By anchoring measurements to NCO/BMO-related geometry, OCT analysis can support more robust estimates of rim loss, cup expansion, and structural change over time ref [57], ref [4].

Taken together, these studies suggest that the future value of OCT-based CAD lies less in reproducing expert labels and more in deriving biomarkers that are anatomically explicit, longitudinally stable, and clinically interpretable. Segmentation remains the enabling layer, but the real objective is biomarker reliability under imaging variability, vessel shadowing, and interobserver disagreement. This progression—from disc and cup contouring to NCO/BMO-centered quantification—illustrates how structural OCT is evolving into a platform for objective glaucoma phenotyping and progression-sensitive ophthalmic biomarkers ref [79], ref [4].

subsections.section_title: Emerging Trends, Synthesis, and Conclusions
subsections.subsection_title: Evolution of Computer-Assisted Diagnostic Reasoning
subsections.content:
The evolution of computer-assisted diagnostic reasoning in medicine provides an instructive backdrop for ophthalmic CAD. Early systems were largely knowledge-driven and symbolic: CASNET/EXPERT formalized causal and hierarchical representations of disease states, while INTERNIST-I demonstrated how large rule-based knowledge bases could generate broad differentials for complex internal-medicine presentations, albeit with clear limitations in explanation, temporal reasoning, and transportability across settings [1], ref [64]. These early efforts established a lasting principle for ophthalmology: diagnostic support is not merely classification, but structured reasoning under uncertainty.

A second transition involved probabilistic and data-informed reasoning. Sequential Bayesian approaches showed how differential diagnosis could be updated as findings accrued, but also exposed the fragility of expert-estimated priors, sensitivities, and specificities [2]. Haug et al. later showed that revising diagnostic logic using a representative clinical database materially changed these parameters and improved system behavior, underscoring that diagnostic reasoning must be calibrated to the target population rather than to expert intuition alone [3]. Related pattern-based systems such as MEDAS and comparative evaluations of computer-based diagnostic aids further reinforced the shift from handcrafted heuristics toward empirically tuned inference [38], [2].

A third phase emphasized prospective evaluation in real clinical workflows. Study-design analyses of computerized support for pneumonia illustrated challenges that remain highly relevant to ophthalmology: low disease prevalence, verification bias, imperfect reference standards, clinician behavior, and the difference between stand-alone accuracy and integrated point-of-care usefulness [4]. Contemporary ophthalmic systems inherit this trajectory: they increasingly fuse image-derived probabilities with longitudinal records and practice context, moving from isolated lesion detection toward deployable reasoning systems whose value depends as much on calibration, workflow integration, and evaluation rigor as on algorithmic performance [48], [50].

subsections.section_title: Emerging Trends, Synthesis, and Conclusions
subsections.subsection_title: Multimodal Data, Pattern Recognition, and Predictive Medicine
subsections.content:
A major emerging trend in ocular CAD is the shift from single-image classifiers toward multimodal learning, in which fundus appearance is interpreted jointly with clinical, demographic, functional, and increasingly genetic data. Early fusion studies already showed that complementary signals can improve diagnostic discrimination beyond any isolated modality, as seen in diabetic retinopathy information fusion, OCT-perimetry integration for glaucoma, and heterogeneous models for pathological myopia diagnosis ref [28], ref [2], ref [3]. In the latter, multiple-kernel learning over fundus, clinical, and SNP data achieved higher accuracy than image-only, clinical-only, or genotype-only models, offering an instructive example of how ophthalmic CAD can move from image recognition to risk modeling ref [2].

This evolution also reframes pattern recognition itself. Rather than detecting a lesion in a single frame, systems increasingly learn disease signatures distributed across structure, phenotype, and host susceptibility. Population-based studies and twin studies in glaucoma, cataract, macular degeneration, and refractive error support the biological plausibility of such models by showing that clinically relevant endophenotypes and disease liability have substantial heritable components ref [4], ref [5], ref [6], ref [7], ref [8], ref [9]. In parallel, statistical learning methods developed for high-dimensional association data, including lasso-based genome-wide modeling and interaction screening, provide a methodological basis for selecting compact predictive biomarker sets from very heterogeneous feature spaces ref [10], ref [11], ref [12].

Viewed together, these developments point toward predictive medicine in ophthalmology: models that estimate future risk, progression propensity, or treatment need by combining imaging biomarkers with systemic and genomic context. Yet translation requires careful attention to cohort shift, missing modalities, cost, and interpretability. The promise is therefore not merely higher AUCs, but clinically actionable stratification that links observed retinal patterns to individualized risk profiles and longitudinal decision support ref [2], ref [13].

subsections.section_title: Emerging Trends, Synthesis, and Conclusions
subsections.subsection_title: Cognitive and Practical Limits in Clinical Decision Systems
subsections.content:
A persistent but underemphasized constraint in ophthalmic CAD is that diagnosis is not only an optimization problem but also a cognitive one. Clinical users must interpret probabilities, images, alerts, and longitudinal trends under bounded attention and working memory; classic cognitive psychology already warned that human processing capacity is limited, particularly when many discrete alternatives or cues must be handled simultaneously ref [83]. This helps explain why rule-heavy expert systems, although influential, often struggled at the point of care despite strong internal logic, as seen in early consultation frameworks such as CASNET/EXPERT, Internist-I, and later database-driven revision systems ref [2], ref [3], ref [4].

In ophthalmology, these limits become practical when CAD outputs proliferate across lesion detectors, segmentation overlays, risk scores, genotype markers, and multimodal summaries. Studies on automated glaucoma support and image-based retinal classification illustrate the promise of algorithmic assistance, but they also imply a risk of cognitive overload if systems expose too many intermediate variables instead of actionable abstractions ref [5], ref [6], ref [7]. More recent fusion strategies, such as combining OCT with perimetry for glaucoma diagnostics or integrating heterogeneous evidence for diabetic retinopathy, improve discriminative performance, yet they further increase interface and workflow complexity unless carefully curated for clinical use ref [8], ref [9].

Practical limits are equally important: data quality shifts, device heterogeneity, incomplete follow-up, referral thresholds, accountability, and trust calibration all shape real-world utility. Experience from computerized decision support outside ophthalmology showed that evaluation must consider workflow, acceptance, and failure modes, not accuracy alone ref [10]. Hence, the next generation of ophthalmic decision systems should prioritize selective disclosure, uncertainty-aware explanations, and tiered recommendations that respect human cognitive bottlenecks while preserving the benefits of multimodal predictive modeling ref [83], ref [11], ref [12].

subsections.section_title: Figures and Tables
subsections.subsection_title: Figures and Tables
subsections.content:
Figures and tables in ocular CAD surveys should do more than summarize results; they should reveal the pipeline structure, imaging modality, target lesion, and evaluation setting. A compact taxonomy figure can map fundus, OCT, slit-lamp, and retro-illumination imaging to major diseases such as diabetic retinopathy, glaucoma, age-related macular degeneration, cataract, and pathological myopia, reflecting the modality-specific workflows described across representative systems for retinal, optic nerve head, and lens analysis ref [4], ref [31], ref [28], ref [33], ref [79], ref [42].

Method-oriented tables are especially valuable when they separate preprocessing, segmentation, feature extraction, and classification stages, since older CAD studies often relied on explicit handcrafted pipelines. For example, diabetic retinopathy tables can distinguish microaneurysm-, exudate-, and screening-level systems ref [8], ref [10], ref [49], while glaucoma tables should separately report disc/cup segmentation, vessel-based cues, stereo analysis, and multimodal fusion ref [54], ref [15], ref [55], ref [27]. Similar disease-specific tables are useful for AMD, cataract, and myopia, where the algorithmic targets differ substantially from lesion detection in DR ref [41], ref [34], ref [24].

To maximize comparability, performance tables should explicitly list dataset source, image count, reference standard, lesion- or image-level endpoint, and metrics such as sensitivity, specificity, AUC, overlap, or cup-to-disc error. Because studies span population screening, clinic-based diagnosis, and progression monitoring, visual summaries should also indicate whether validation is internal, cross-dataset, or longitudinal ref [46], ref [51]. Such figure and table design helps readers identify genuine methodological advances rather than superficial metric gains.
